Growth Models

 Analysis of longitudinal student assessment data (i.e., growth
 models/value-added models) is not particularly new.
 Tennessee has been analyzing state longitudinal assessment data
 as part of its value-added system for almost 20 years.
 These analyses were/are almost exclusively directed toward
 accountability/evaluation.
 Student growth percentiles were developed to provide a vocabulary
 to talk about student growth that wasn’t exclusively about
 evaluation/accountability.

Growth Models

 With a heavy emphasis on accountability, the bottom line for states
 is data for accountability purposes.
 This impoverishes the potential uses of data and supports fixed
 mindset thinking about data use in education.
 The challenge: Use data in ways that promotes a growth mindset in
 all stakeholders: students, parents, teachers, ...
 Growth models have more potential to do this than simple status
 measures.
 How can this potential use of growth models be realized?

Describing Student Growth

 Measuring student growth, even with a vertical scale, is not a simple
 task.
 Some believe a vertical scale simplifies the task of measuring
 student growth.
 Even with an interval (or ratio) scale, growth is not easy to interpret.
 Consider, for example, height.
 A child might grow 4 inches between ages 3 and 4.
 4 inches is a well understood quantity.
 The 4 inch increase becomes really meaningful only when understood
 alongside the growth of other 3 to 4 year olds.
 Student growth percentiles were developed to provide a normative
 context for describing student
 growth.[Betebenner, 2008, Betebenner, 2009]
